chunks: Ali ibn Muhammad ibn Bundar and others, from Ahmad ibn Abi Abdullah, from his father, from Abdullah ibn al-Qasim, from a man from the people of Saabat, who said:

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said to Ammar: 'O Ammar, you are a lord of much wealth?' He said: 'Yes, may I be sacrificed for you.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'So do you pay what Allah has obligated upon you from the zakat?' He said, 'Yes.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'So do you take out the known (amount) from your wealth?' He said, 'Yes.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'So you give it to your relatives?' He said, 'Yes.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'So you give it to your brethren?' He said, 'Yes.' So he (peace be upon him) said: 'O Ammar! The wealth perishes, and the body decays, but the deeds remain, and the Judge is Alive and does not die. O Ammar! Whatever you send forward, does not leave you behind; whatever you delay does not catch up with you.'
ai.seo_question: What did Imam al-Sadiq teach about the relationship between wealth, deeds, and the afterlife?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi highlights the triad of financial piety—zakat, maintaining kinship ties (silat al-rahim), and charity to brethren—as the means to transcend the impermanence of wealth and the body. Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) uses this dialogue to underscore the eschatological reality that deeds are the only enduring currency before the Ever-Living Judge (al-Dayan), a concept deeply rooted in Shia reflections on the transient nature of worldly life (zahir al-hayat) versus the eternal hereafter (akhira).
